slides.narration: In this part we meet vectors, quantities that need a direction as well as a size. We write them with unit vectors, multiply them by numbers, and add and subtract them by the triangle and parallelogram laws. We derive the magnitude and direction of the resultant and look at its special cases.

slides.heading: Scalars and vectors
slides.body_md: A **scalar** has magnitude only; a **vector** has magnitude **and** direction and obeys the laws of vector addition.
bullets: Scalars add like numbers: 3 kg + 4 kg = 7 kg. Vectors add by the triangle law: 3 m east and 4 m north give 5 m at an angle.
A vector is drawn as an arrow: length = magnitude, arrowhead = direction. We write $\vec{A}$ and its magnitude $|\vec{A}|$ or $A$.
Electric current has a direction in a wire but is a **scalar**: currents add arithmetically, not by the parallelogram law.
Multiplying or dividing by a scalar changes the magnitude, never the line of action (except for a sign).

slides.narration: A scalar is described by a number and a unit alone, like mass or time. A vector needs a direction too, and combines by the triangle law. We draw a vector as an arrow whose length shows the magnitude. Electric current has a sense along the wire, but currents add like ordinary numbers, so current is a scalar.

slides.heading: Position and displacement vectors
slides.body_md: A **position vector** $\vec{r}$ joins the origin $O$ to a point; the **displacement** joins one position to another.
bullets: Displacement depends only on the initial and final positions, not on the path; the distance travelled is a scalar and can be larger.
In a plane $\vec{r} = (x, y)$; in space $\vec{r} = (x, y, z)$. The displacement from $P$ to $Q$ is $\overrightarrow{PQ} = \vec{r}_Q - \vec{r}_P$.
If the end point is the start point, the displacement is the null vector.

slides.narration: A position vector starts at the origin and ends at the point. The displacement from one point to another is the final position vector minus the initial position vector. It depends only on the end points, not on the route, and it is zero for a complete round trip. The distance travelled is a scalar and can be larger than the size of the displacement.

slides.narration: The displacement is the final position minus the initial position, which is four metres along x and three metres along y. Its magnitude is the square root of sixteen plus nine, which is five metres. The angle with the x axis has tangent three over four, so it is about thirty six point nine degrees above the axis.

slides.heading: Equal, negative, null and coplanar vectors
slides.body_md: Four ideas you will use all the time:
bullets: **Equal vectors:** same magnitude and same direction. A vector can be shifted parallel to itself without change.
**Negative vector:** $-\vec{A}$ has the magnitude of $\vec{A}$ and the opposite direction; $\vec{A} + (-\vec{A}) = \vec{0}$.
**Null vector** $\vec{0}$: zero magnitude, no definite direction. It is a vector, not the number zero.
**Coplanar vectors** lie in one plane. Any two vectors, and their sum, are always coplanar; three vectors need not be.

slides.narration: Equal vectors have the same magnitude and direction, wherever they are drawn. The negative of a vector has the same size and the opposite direction, and adding the two gives the null vector, which has zero magnitude and no definite direction. Vectors are coplanar if they can be drawn in one plane. Two vectors and their sum are always coplanar.

slides.heading: Unit vectors î, ĵ, k̂
slides.body_md: A **unit vector** has magnitude 1, no unit and no dimension; it only shows a direction. $\hat{\imath}$, $\hat{\jmath}$ and $\hat{k}$ point along $+x$, $+y$ and $+z$.
bullets: $A_x$, $A_y$, $A_z$ are the **components** of $\vec{A}$; $A_x\hat{\imath}$ is the part of $\vec{A}$ along $x$ and so on.
$\hat{\imath}$, $\hat{\jmath}$, $\hat{k}$ are mutually perpendicular and each has magnitude 1.
Any vector in space is a sum of three vectors along the axes. In a plane, $A_z = 0$.

slides.narration: A unit vector has magnitude one and only shows direction. The unit vectors i hat, j hat and k hat point along the x, y and z axes and are mutually perpendicular. Any vector can be written as A x times i hat plus A y times j hat plus A z times k hat, where the three numbers are its components.

slides.heading: Magnitude and the unit vector along A
slides.body_md: The magnitude comes from Pythagoras applied twice; dividing by it gives the unit vector.
bullets: Example: $\vec{A} = 2\hat{\imath} + 3\hat{\jmath} + 6\hat{k}$ has $|\vec{A}| = \sqrt{4 + 9 + 36} = 7$ and $\hat{A} = (2\hat{\imath} + 3\hat{\jmath} + 6\hat{k})/7$.
The magnitude of any unit vector is $1$; the three components of $\hat{A}$ are the direction cosines.
A vector of magnitude $F$ along $\hat{A}$ is $F\hat{A}$.

slides.narration: The magnitude of a vector is the square root of the sum of the squares of its components. For two, three and six, that is the square root of forty nine, which is seven. Dividing the vector by its magnitude gives the unit vector in its direction. A vector of magnitude F along that direction is simply F times the unit vector.

slides.heading: Worked example 2: a kite string
slides.body_md: A kite is displaced by $\vec{A} = 4\hat{\imath}-3\hat{\jmath}+12\hat{k}$ m. Find $|\vec{A}|$, the unit vector $\hat{A}$ and the vector of magnitude 26 m along $-\vec{A}$.
bullets: $\hat{A} = \dfrac{4\hat{\imath}-3\hat{\jmath}+12\hat{k}}{13}$; check: $\dfrac{16 + 9 + 144}{169} = 1$.
Along $-\vec{A}$ with magnitude 26 m: $-26\hat{A} = -2(4\hat{\imath}-3\hat{\jmath}+12\hat{k}) = -8\hat{\imath}+6\hat{\jmath}-24\hat{k}$ m.

visual.alt: Table with the magnitude and the unit vector of the vector 4 i minus 3 j plus 12 k

slides.narration: The magnitude is the square root of sixteen plus nine plus one hundred and forty four, which is thirteen metres. Dividing the vector by thirteen gives the unit vector. A vector of magnitude twenty six metres in the opposite direction is minus twenty six times the unit vector, which is minus two times the original vector.

slides.heading: Multiplying a vector by a real number
slides.body_md: For a real number $\lambda$, $\lambda\vec{A}$ is a vector of magnitude $|\lambda| A$.
bullets: If $\lambda > 0$ it points along $\vec{A}$; if $\lambda < 0$ it points opposite to $\vec{A}$; if $\lambda = 0$ it is the null vector.
In components: $\lambda\vec{A} = \lambda A_x\,\hat{\imath} + \lambda A_y\,\hat{\jmath} + \lambda A_z\,\hat{k}$.
Two non-zero vectors are **parallel** (or antiparallel) when one is a multiple of the other: $\vec{B} = \lambda\vec{A}$.
Dividing by a number is multiplying by its reciprocal: $\hat{A} = \dfrac{1}{A}\vec{A}$.

slides.heading: Triangle and parallelogram laws
slides.body_md: Two ways to draw the same sum $\vec{R} = \vec{A} + \vec{B}$:
bullets: **Triangle law:** if two vectors are drawn head to tail as two sides of a triangle, their sum is the third side drawn from the tail of the first to the head of the second.
**Parallelogram law:** if two vectors are drawn from a common point as adjacent sides of a parallelogram, their sum is the diagonal through that point.
The sum is called the **resultant**; the order of addition does not change it. (The proof of commutative and associative laws is not required.)
Subtracting: $\vec{A} - \vec{B} = \vec{A} + (-\vec{B})$.

So alpha is the inverse tangent of that ratio, measured from the first vector. The angle with the second vector is theta minus alpha. With five, four and sixty degrees, the resultant is root sixty one and alpha is about twenty six degrees.

slides.heading: Special cases of the resultant
slides.body_md: Put the angle $\theta$ into $R^2 = A^2 + B^2 + 2AB\cos\theta$:
bullets: $\theta = 0^\circ$: $R = A + B$, the largest value; $\theta = 180^\circ$: $R = |A - B|$, the smallest. So $|A - B| \le R \le A + B$.
$\theta = 90^\circ$: $R = \sqrt{A^2 + B^2}$ and $\tan\alpha = B/A$.
$A = B$: $R = 2A\cos(\theta/2)$ and $\alpha = \theta/2$ (the diagonal of a rhombus bisects the angle); at $120^\circ$, $R = A$.
Three vectors that form a closed triangle taken in order add to the null vector.

slides.narration: When the vectors point the same way the resultant is the sum of the magnitudes, the largest possible. When they point oppositely it is the difference, the smallest. At right angles it is the square root of the sum of squares. If the two vectors are equal, the resultant bisects the angle between them, and at one hundred and twenty degrees it equals each of them.

slides.heading: Worked example 3: two ropes on a barge
slides.body_md: Two ropes pull a barge with forces of 7 N and 8 N, 60$^\circ$ apart. Find the magnitude and direction of the resultant force.
bullets: $\tan\alpha = \dfrac{8\sin 60^\circ}{7 + 8\cos 60^\circ} = \dfrac{6.93}{11} = 0.630$, so $\alpha = 32.2^\circ$ from the 7 N rope.
Angle with the 8 N rope: $60^\circ - 32.2^\circ = 27.8^\circ$, so the resultant lies nearer the larger force.

visual.alt: Table with the resultant of a 7 newton and an 8 newton force at 60 degrees: magnitude 13 newtons and angle about 32.2 degrees from the 7 newton force

slides.narration: Using the law just derived, R squared is forty nine plus sixty four plus fifty six, which is one hundred and sixty nine, so the resultant is thirteen newtons. The tangent of alpha is six point nine three over eleven, so alpha is about thirty two point two degrees from the smaller force. The resultant lies closer to the larger force, as it should.

slides.heading: Subtraction and the two diagonals
slides.body_md: The two diagonals of a parallelogram on $\vec{A}$ and $\vec{B}$ are the sum and the difference.
bullets: The diagonal from the common point is $\vec{A} + \vec{B}$; the other diagonal, drawn from the head of $\vec{B}$ to the head of $\vec{A}$, is $\vec{A} - \vec{B}$.
Replace $\theta$ by $180^\circ - \theta$ in the law of the sum, since $-\vec{B}$ makes that angle with $\vec{A}$.
In unit-vector form, add or subtract component by component.
Adding the squares of the diagonals gives $|\vec{A} + \vec{B}|^2 + |\vec{A} - \vec{B}|^2 = 2(A^2 + B^2)$.

slides.heading: Worked example 4: sum and difference in unit-vector form
slides.body_md: $\vec{A} = 5\hat{\imath}-\hat{\jmath}+4\hat{k}$ and $\vec{B} = -3\hat{\imath}+4\hat{\jmath}+2\hat{k}$. Find $\vec{A} + \vec{B}$, $\vec{A} - \vec{B}$ and their magnitudes.
bullets: $\vec{A} + \vec{B} = (5 + (-3))\hat{\imath} + (-1 + 4)\hat{\jmath} + (4 + 2)\hat{k} = 2\hat{\imath}+3\hat{\jmath}+6\hat{k}$; $|\vec{A} + \vec{B}| = \sqrt{49} = 7$.
$\vec{A} - \vec{B} = (5 - (-3))\hat{\imath} + (-1 - 4)\hat{\jmath} + (4 - 2)\hat{k} = 8\hat{\imath}-5\hat{\jmath}+2\hat{k}$; $|\vec{A} - \vec{B}| = \sqrt{93} = 9.64$.

slides.narration: Add the matching components to get the sum, which has components two, three and six and magnitude seven. Subtract them to get the difference, with components eight, minus five and two, and magnitude about nine point six four. As a check, the squares of the two magnitudes add up to twice the sum of the squares of the original magnitudes.

slides.narration: In this part we split a vector into rectangular components, use components to add many vectors, and meet the two products of vectors. The dot product gives a scalar, like work. The cross product gives a vector, like torque. We finish with their special cases at zero, ninety and one hundred and eighty degrees.

slides.heading: Resolution into rectangular components
slides.body_md: **Resolving** a vector means replacing it by two or more vectors, **components**, whose sum is the vector. Along perpendicular axes:
bullets: $\theta$ is the angle with the $x$-axis; if it is measured from the $y$-axis, the cosine and sine swap.
$\vec{A} = A_x\hat{\imath} + A_y\hat{\jmath}$; the components and $\vec{A}$ form a right-angled triangle, so $A^2 = A_x^2 + A_y^2$.
A component can be positive, negative or zero, and never exceeds the magnitude of the vector.
Resolve along any two perpendicular directions that suit the problem, for example along and across a slope.

slides.narration: To resolve a vector, replace it by two perpendicular components. If theta is the angle with the x axis, the x component is A cos theta and the y component is A sin theta. The vector is the hypotenuse of the right triangle, so its magnitude is the square root of the sum of the squares, and the tangent of theta is the ratio of the components.

slides.heading: Worked example 5: pulling a handcart
slides.body_md: A porter pulls a handcart with a rope that exerts 50 N at 30$^\circ$ above the horizontal. Find the horizontal and vertical components.
bullets: $F_x = F\cos\theta = 50\cos 30^\circ = 43.3$ N (this part moves the cart forward).
$F_y = F\sin\theta = 50\sin 30^\circ = 25.0$ N (this part lifts the rope end and eases the load).
Check: $\sqrt{43.3^2 + 25.0^2} = 50.0$ N, the original force.

visual.alt: Table with the rectangular components of a 50 newton force at 30 degrees, recovering the magnitude and the angle

slides.narration: The horizontal component is fifty times cosine of thirty degrees, about forty three point three newtons, and it moves the cart forward. The vertical component is fifty times sine of thirty degrees, which is twenty five newtons, and it partly lifts the load. Combining them again gives back fifty newtons.

slides.heading: Resolution in three dimensions
slides.body_md: In space, $\vec{A} = A_x\hat{\imath} + A_y\hat{\jmath} + A_z\hat{k}$; the components are the edges of a box whose diagonal is $\vec{A}$.
bullets: $\alpha$, $\beta$, $\gamma$ are the angles that $\vec{A}$ makes with the $x$, $y$ and $z$ axes; the cosines are the **direction cosines**.
The unit vector is $\hat{A} = \cos\alpha\,\hat{\imath} + \cos\beta\,\hat{\jmath} + \cos\gamma\,\hat{k}$, so $\cos^2\alpha + \cos^2\beta + \cos^2\gamma = 1$.
Add, subtract and scale 3-D vectors component by component.

slides.heading: Resultant from rectangular components
slides.body_md: To add many coplanar vectors, add their components. The resultant and its angle follow from the sums:
bullets: $\varphi$ is the angle of $\vec{R}$ with the $x$-axis; the signs of $\Sigma X$ and $\Sigma Y$ tell the quadrant (a calculator gives only $-90^\circ$ to $90^\circ$).
For two vectors this agrees with $R^2 = A^2 + B^2 + 2AB\cos\theta$.
The resultant is zero when $\Sigma X = 0$ and $\Sigma Y = 0$: the forces balance.

rows: Draw the axes and mark each force with its angle from +x
Resolve each force: X = F cos θ, Y = F sin θ (keep the signs)
Add: ΣX = X₁ + X₂ + …, ΣY = Y₁ + Y₂ + …
tan φ = ΣY/ΣX; fix the quadrant from the signs of ΣX and ΣY

math: \Sigma X = A_x + B_x + C_x + \cdots, \qquad \Sigma Y = A_y + B_y + C_y + \cdots
slides.narration: To find the resultant of many vectors, resolve each along x and y, add all the x components, add all the y components, and combine the two sums by Pythagoras. The tangent of the angle is the sum of y over the sum of x, and the signs show the quadrant. If both sums are zero the vectors balance and the resultant is the null vector.

slides.heading: Scalar (dot) product
slides.body_md: The **scalar product** of $\vec{A}$ and $\vec{B}$, with angle $\theta$ between them, is a **scalar**:
bullets: It is the magnitude of one vector times the **projection** of the other on it: $A(B\cos\theta)$.
**Work** is the standard example: only the component of the force along the displacement does work, so $W = \vec{F}\cdot\vec{s}$.
It is positive for $\theta < 90^\circ$, zero at $90^\circ$ and negative for $\theta > 90^\circ$.
Another use: power $P = \vec{F}\cdot\vec{v}$.

slides.narration: The scalar or dot product of two vectors is the product of their magnitudes and the cosine of the angle between them. The answer is a scalar. It equals the magnitude of one vector times the projection of the other along it. Work is the standard example: only the part of the force along the displacement does work. The dot product is positive below ninety degrees, zero at ninety, and negative above.

slides.heading: Properties and component form of the dot product
slides.body_md: From $\vec{A}\cdot\vec{B} = AB\cos\theta$ and the unit-vector products, the component form follows:
bullets: $\hat{\imath}\cdot\hat{\imath} = \hat{\jmath}\cdot\hat{\jmath} = \hat{k}\cdot\hat{k} = 1$ ($\theta = 0$) and $\hat{\imath}\cdot\hat{\jmath} = \hat{\jmath}\cdot\hat{k} = \hat{k}\cdot\hat{\imath} = 0$ ($\theta = 90^\circ$).
Expand $(A_x\hat{\imath} + A_y\hat{\jmath} + A_z\hat{k})\cdot(B_x\hat{\imath} + B_y\hat{\jmath} + B_z\hat{k})$ with the distributive law; the cross terms vanish.
$\vec{A}\cdot\vec{A} = A^2$. Two non-zero vectors are **perpendicular** when $\vec{A}\cdot\vec{B} = 0$.

headers: Dot product A·B = A B cos θ

visual.alt: Table of the properties of the scalar product, including its component form and the angle formula

slides.narration: The dot product is commutative and distributive. The dot product of a unit vector with itself is one, and with a different unit vector it is zero. Multiplying out the components, only the matching terms survive, so the dot product is A x B x plus A y B y plus A z B z. The cosine of the angle between two vectors is the dot product divided by the product of the magnitudes.

slides.heading: Worked example 8: work and the angle between two vectors
slides.body_md: A force $\vec{F} = 2\hat{\imath}-3\hat{\jmath}+4\hat{k}$ N moves a body through $\vec{s} = 5\hat{\imath}+2\hat{\jmath}+3\hat{k}$ m. Find the work done and the angle between $\vec{F}$ and $\vec{s}$.
bullets: $\cos\theta = \dfrac{16}{5.39 \times 6.16} = 0.482$, so $\theta = 61.2^\circ$ (acute, so the work is positive).

slides.narration: Multiply the matching components and add: ten minus six plus twelve, which is sixteen joules. The magnitudes are the square roots of twenty nine and thirty eight. The cosine of the angle is sixteen divided by their product, about zero point four eight two, so the angle is about sixty one point two degrees. It is acute, which matches the positive work.

slides.heading: Vector (cross) product
slides.body_md: The **vector product** of $\vec{A}$ and $\vec{B}$ is a **vector** of magnitude $AB\sin\theta$:
bullets: $\hat{n}$ is perpendicular to the plane of $\vec{A}$ and $\vec{B}$, given by the **right-hand screw rule**: turn a right-handed screw from $\vec{A}$ to $\vec{B}$ through the smaller angle; it advances along $\hat{n}$.
The magnitude equals the **area of the parallelogram** on $\vec{A}$ and $\vec{B}$.
**Torque** is the standard example: $\vec{\tau} = \vec{r}\times\vec{F}$, with $\vec{r}$ from the axis to the point of application of the force.

slides.narration: The vector or cross product of two vectors has magnitude A B sin theta and a direction perpendicular to both, given by the right hand screw rule. Its magnitude equals the area of the parallelogram on the two vectors. Torque is the standard example: the cross product of the position vector from the axis with the force.

slides.heading: Properties and component form of the cross product
slides.body_md: Reversing the order reverses the direction; unit vectors follow a cyclic pattern.
bullets: $\hat{\imath}\times\hat{\jmath} = \hat{k}$, $\hat{\jmath}\times\hat{k} = \hat{\imath}$, $\hat{k}\times\hat{\imath} = \hat{\jmath}$; $\hat{\imath}\times\hat{\imath} = 0$ and so on.
$\vec{B}\times\vec{A} = -(\vec{A}\times\vec{B})$: the cross product is **not** commutative. $\vec{A}\times\vec{A} = \vec{0}$.
Distributive: $\vec{A}\times(\vec{B} + \vec{C}) = \vec{A}\times\vec{B} + \vec{A}\times\vec{C}$.

headers: Cross product A × B = A B sin θ n̂
rows: perpendicular to both A and B; right-hand screw rule
A × (B + C) = A × B + A × C
î × ĵ = k̂, ĵ × k̂ = î, k̂ × î = ĵ; reversed order gives the negative; î × î = 0
A × B = (A_yB_z − A_zB_y) î + (A_zBₓ − AₓB_z) ĵ + (AₓB_y − A_yBₓ) k̂

math: \vec{A}\times\vec{B} = \begin{vmatrix} \hat{\imath} & \hat{\jmath} & \hat{k} \\ A_x & A_y & A_z \\ B_x & B_y & B_z \end{vmatrix}
slides.narration: Reversing the order of the cross product reverses its direction, so it is not commutative. A vector crossed with itself is zero. For the unit vectors, i hat cross j hat is k hat, j hat cross k hat is i hat, and k hat cross i hat is j hat, and the reverse orders give negatives. Multiplying out gives the component form, which you can remember as a three by three determinant.

slides.heading: Dot and cross products at 0°, 90° and 180°
slides.body_md: Two products, two special-angle patterns:
bullets: **Parallel** ($\theta = 0^\circ$): $\vec{A}\cdot\vec{B} = AB$ (largest) and $\vec{A}\times\vec{B} = \vec{0}$.
**Perpendicular** ($\theta = 90^\circ$): $\vec{A}\cdot\vec{B} = 0$ and $|\vec{A}\times\vec{B}| = AB$ (largest).
**Antiparallel** ($\theta = 180^\circ$): $\vec{A}\cdot\vec{B} = -AB$ and $\vec{A}\times\vec{B} = \vec{0}$.
Dot product: a scalar, commutative, measures how much two vectors point the same way. Cross product: a vector, not commutative, measures how much they are at right angles.

visual.alt: Table of the dot and cross products for angles of 0, 90 and 180 degrees

slides.narration: At zero degrees the dot product is largest and the cross product vanishes. At ninety degrees the dot product vanishes and the cross product is largest. At one hundred and eighty degrees the dot product is the most negative and the cross product again vanishes. The dot product is a commutative scalar; the cross product is a vector that changes sign when the order is reversed.

slides.heading: Summary — Part 2
slides.body_md: Key results:

rows: Aₓ = A cos θ, A_y = A sin θ; A = √(Aₓ² + A_y²); 3-D: add A_z
cos α = Aₓ/A, … ; cos²α + cos²β + cos²γ = 1
A·B = AB cos θ = AₓBₓ + A_yB_y + A_zB_z; work W = F·s
A × B = AB sin θ n̂ (right-hand screw); torque τ = r × F

slides.narration: To sum up. Resolve a vector into A cos theta and A sin theta, and recover its size by Pythagoras. For many forces, add the x and y components separately. The dot product is a scalar, A B cos theta, equal to the sum of products of matching components, and gives work. The cross product is a vector of magnitude A B sin theta along the right hand screw direction, and gives torque.

slides.heading: Exam tips — Part 2
bullets: Draw the axes and mark the angle before resolving; check with $\sqrt{A_x^2 + A_y^2} = A$.
When the angle is measured from the $y$-axis the components swap: $A_x = A\sin\theta$.
Write the dot product as a sum of three products and the cross product as a determinant, line by line; give the unit of work (J) or torque (N m) and the direction of $\vec{\tau}$.
State the right-hand screw rule when asked for the direction of a cross product.
Common mistakes: using $\tan^{-1}$ without checking the quadrant; $\vec{A}\times\vec{B} = \vec{B}\times\vec{A}$; treating the dot product as a vector.

notes.title: Vectors — Notes

sections.heading: 1. Scalars and vectors; position and displacement vectors; equal, null and coplanar vectors
sections.body_md:
- A **scalar** has magnitude only (mass, time, speed, work, energy, power). A **vector** has magnitude and direction and obeys the laws of vector addition (displacement, velocity, force, momentum, torque). Electric current has a sense but adds arithmetically, so it is a scalar.
- A vector is drawn as an arrow: length = magnitude, arrowhead = direction; written $\vec{A}$, magnitude $|\vec{A}| = A$.
- **Position vector** $\vec{r}$: from the origin to a point. **Displacement** $\Delta\vec{r} = \vec{r}_2 - \vec{r}_1$ depends only on the end points. A drone from $P(2, 1)$ to $Q(6, 4)$ m has $\Delta\vec{r} = (4, 3)$ m, magnitude 5 m, at 36.9° to the $x$-axis.
- **Equal vectors:** same magnitude and direction. **Negative vector** $-\vec{A}$: opposite direction. **Null vector** $\vec{0}$: zero magnitude, no definite direction; $\vec{A} + (-\vec{A}) = \vec{0}$ (a complete round trip has zero displacement). **Coplanar vectors** lie in one plane; any two vectors and their sum are coplanar.

sections.heading: 2. Unit vectors î, ĵ, k̂; magnitude; multiplication by a real number
sections.body_md:
- A **unit vector** has magnitude 1, no unit and no dimension; $\hat{\imath}$, $\hat{\jmath}$, $\hat{k}$ point along $+x$, $+y$, $+z$ and are mutually perpendicular. Any vector is $\vec{A} = A_x\hat{\imath} + A_y\hat{\jmath} + A_z\hat{k}$.
- Magnitude $|\vec{A}| = \sqrt{A_x^2 + A_y^2 + A_z^2}$; unit vector $\hat{A} = \vec{A}/|\vec{A}|$. For $\vec{A} = 4\hat{\imath}-3\hat{\jmath}+12\hat{k}$ m: $|\vec{A}| = 13$ m and $\hat{A} = (4\hat{\imath}-3\hat{\jmath}+12\hat{k})/13$.
- **Multiplication by a real number:** $\lambda\vec{A}$ has magnitude $|\lambda|A$, direction of $\vec{A}$ if $\lambda > 0$, opposite if $\lambda < 0$, and is $\vec{0}$ if $\lambda = 0$. In components every component is multiplied by $\lambda$. Two vectors are parallel when $\vec{B} = \lambda\vec{A}$.

sections.heading: 3. Addition and subtraction: triangle and parallelogram laws; resultant; special cases
sections.body_md:
- **Triangle law:** the sum of two vectors drawn head to tail is the third side of the triangle. **Parallelogram law:** two vectors drawn from a point as adjacent sides have the diagonal through that point as their sum. (Proof of the commutative and associative laws is not required.)
- With $\theta$ between $\vec{A}$ and $\vec{B}$: $R = \sqrt{A^2 + B^2 + 2AB\cos\theta}$ and $\tan\alpha = \dfrac{B\sin\theta}{A + B\cos\theta}$, $\alpha$ measured from $\vec{A}$. Derivation: drop $SN \perp OP$ produced; $ON = A + B\cos\theta$, $SN = B\sin\theta$; Pythagoras in $\triangle ONS$.
- Special cases: $\theta = 0^\circ$, $R = A + B$ (maximum); $90^\circ$, $R = \sqrt{A^2 + B^2}$; $180^\circ$, $R = |A - B|$ (minimum); equal magnitudes, $R = 2A\cos(\theta/2)$ along the bisector. Always $|A - B| \le R \le A + B$.
- Example: 7 N and 8 N at 60° give $R = 13$ N at 32.2° from the 7 N force.
- **Subtraction:** $\vec{A} - \vec{B} = \vec{A} + (-\vec{B})$; the two diagonals of the parallelogram are $\vec{A} + \vec{B}$ and $\vec{A} - \vec{B}$; $|\vec{A} - \vec{B}| = \sqrt{A^2 + B^2 - 2AB\cos\theta}$. In unit-vector form add or subtract component by component: $5\hat{\imath}-\hat{\jmath}+4\hat{k}$ and $-3\hat{\imath}+4\hat{\jmath}+2\hat{k}$ give $2\hat{\imath}+3\hat{\jmath}+6\hat{k}$ and $8\hat{\imath}-5\hat{\jmath}+2\hat{k}$.

sections.heading: 4. Resolution of a vector; rectangular components and the resultant
sections.body_md:
- **Resolution** replaces a vector by components whose sum is the vector. Along perpendicular axes, with $\theta$ from the $x$-axis: $A_x = A\cos\theta$, $A_y = A\sin\theta$, $A = \sqrt{A_x^2 + A_y^2}$, $\tan\theta = A_y/A_x$. A 50 N pull at 30° has components 43.3 N and 25.0 N.
- **In 3-D:** $A = \sqrt{A_x^2 + A_y^2 + A_z^2}$; direction cosines $\cos\alpha = A_x/A$, $\cos\beta = A_y/A$, $\cos\gamma = A_z/A$ with $\cos^2\alpha + \cos^2\beta + \cos^2\gamma = 1$. For $2\hat{\imath}+3\hat{\jmath}+6\hat{k}$ the angles are 73.4°, 64.6°, 31.0°.
- **Resultant from components:** $\Sigma X$ and $\Sigma Y$ are the sums of the components; $R = \sqrt{(\Sigma X)^2 + (\Sigma Y)^2}$, $\tan\varphi = \Sigma Y/\Sigma X$ with the quadrant from the signs. Three pulls of 40 N, 30 N, 20 N at 0°, 90°, 210° give $R = 30.2$ N at 41.4°.
- If $\Sigma X = \Sigma Y = 0$ the vectors add to the null vector (equilibrium).

The cosines of the angles a vector makes with the three axes.

sections.heading: 5. Scalar (dot) product and vector (cross) product
sections.body_md:
- **Dot product** $\vec{A}\cdot\vec{B} = AB\cos\theta$ (a scalar): magnitude of one times the projection of the other. Work $W = \vec{F}\cdot\vec{s}$; power $P = \vec{F}\cdot\vec{v}$. Commutative, distributive; $\vec{A}\cdot\vec{A} = A^2$; $\hat{\imath}\cdot\hat{\imath} = 1$, $\hat{\imath}\cdot\hat{\jmath} = 0$ etc.; component form $A_xB_x + A_yB_y + A_zB_z$; angle $\cos\theta = \vec{A}\cdot\vec{B}/(AB)$; perpendicular if the product is zero. For $2\hat{\imath}-3\hat{\jmath}+4\hat{k}$ N and $5\hat{\imath}+2\hat{\jmath}+3\hat{k}$ m: $W = 16$ J, $\theta = 61.2^\circ$.
- **Cross product** $\vec{A}\times\vec{B} = AB\sin\theta\,\hat{n}$ (a vector): $\hat{n}$ by the right-hand screw rule; magnitude = area of the parallelogram. Torque $\vec{\tau} = \vec{r}\times\vec{F}$. Not commutative: $\vec{B}\times\vec{A} = -\vec{A}\times\vec{B}$; $\vec{A}\times\vec{A} = \vec{0}$; $\hat{\imath}\times\hat{\jmath} = \hat{k}$, $\hat{\jmath}\times\hat{k} = \hat{\imath}$, $\hat{k}\times\hat{\imath} = \hat{\jmath}$; determinant form for components. For $3\hat{\imath}+\hat{\jmath}-2\hat{k}$ and $\hat{\imath}-2\hat{\jmath}+2\hat{k}$: $\vec{A}\times\vec{B} = -2\hat{\imath}-8\hat{\jmath}-7\hat{k}$. A 40 N force at right angles to a 0.3 m arm gives $\tau = 12$ N m.
- **Special angles:** $0^\circ$: $A\cdot B = AB$, $A\times B = 0$; $90^\circ$: $A\cdot B = 0$, $|A\times B| = AB$; $180^\circ$: $A\cdot B = -AB$, $A\times B = 0$.

key_terms.definition_md: A·B = AB cos θ, a scalar; gives work as F·s.
A × B = AB sin θ n̂, a vector perpendicular to both; gives torque as r × F.
The direction of A × B is the way a right-handed screw advances when turned from A to B.

provenance.author: claude-sonnet-5-5 (subject-producer chapter writer; reviewed by claude-opus-5-5)

cards.front_md: Define a vector. Which test separates a vector from a scalar that has a direction?
cards.back_md: A vector has magnitude and direction and obeys the vector addition laws; current has a sense but adds like a number, so it is a scalar.

cards.front_md: What is a displacement vector?
cards.back_md: The vector from the initial to the final position, $\vec{r}_2 - \vec{r}_1$; it does not depend on the path.

cards.front_md: Define a position vector.
cards.back_md: A vector from the origin to the point.

cards.front_md: When are two vectors equal?
cards.back_md: When they have the same magnitude and the same direction, wherever they are drawn.

cards.front_md: What is a null vector?
cards.back_md: A vector of zero magnitude and no definite direction, e.g. the displacement after a round trip.

cards.front_md: When are vectors coplanar?
cards.back_md: When they lie in one plane (or can be drawn in one plane by shifting them parallel to themselves).

cards.front_md: Are two vectors always coplanar?
cards.back_md: Yes. Any two vectors, with their sum, lie in one plane; three vectors need not.

cards.front_md: What is the negative of a vector?
cards.back_md: A vector of the same magnitude in the opposite direction; $\vec{A} + (-\vec{A}) = \vec{0}$.

cards.front_md: What is a unit vector? State its magnitude and dimension.
cards.back_md: A vector giving direction only; magnitude 1, no unit, dimensionless.

cards.front_md: Name the unit vectors along x, y and z.
cards.back_md: $\hat{\imath}$, $\hat{\jmath}$ and $\hat{k}$.

cards.front_md: Write the magnitude of $A_x\hat{\imath} + A_y\hat{\jmath} + A_z\hat{k}$.
Write the unit vector along $\vec{A}$.
cards.back_md: $\hat{A} = \vec{A}/|\vec{A}|$.

cards.front_md: What does $\lambda\vec{A}$ look like for $\lambda < 0$?
cards.back_md: Magnitude $|\lambda|A$ and direction opposite to $\vec{A}$.

cards.front_md: State the triangle law of vector addition.
cards.back_md: If two vectors are drawn head to tail as two sides of a triangle, their sum is the third side from the tail of the first to the head of the second.

cards.front_md: State the parallelogram law.
cards.back_md: If two vectors are drawn from a point as adjacent sides of a parallelogram, their sum is the diagonal through that point.

cards.front_md: Write the magnitude of the resultant of $\vec{A}$ and $\vec{B}$ at angle $\theta$.
cards.back_md: $R = \sqrt{A^2 + B^2 + 2AB\cos\theta}$.

cards.front_md: Write the direction of the resultant.
cards.back_md: $\tan\alpha = \dfrac{B\sin\theta}{A + B\cos\theta}$, $\alpha$ measured from $\vec{A}$.

cards.front_md: What is R when the vectors are parallel, perpendicular and antiparallel?
Between which limits does the resultant of A and B lie?
cards.back_md: $|A - B| \le R \le A + B$.

cards.front_md: What are the diagonals of a parallelogram on $\vec{A}$ and $\vec{B}$?
cards.back_md: The sum $\vec{A} + \vec{B}$ and the difference $\vec{A} - \vec{B}$.

cards.front_md: Write the rectangular components of a vector A at angle θ to the x-axis.
cards.back_md: $A_x = A\cos\theta$ and $A_y = A\sin\theta$.

cards.front_md: How do you recover A and θ from the components?
cards.back_md: $A = \sqrt{A_x^2 + A_y^2}$ and $\tan\theta = A_y/A_x$ (check the quadrant).

cards.front_md: What are the direction cosines of a vector?
cards.back_md: $A_x/A$, $A_y/A$, $A_z/A$, the cosines of the angles with the axes; their squares add to 1.

cards.front_md: How do you find the resultant of several coplanar vectors?
cards.back_md: Add the x components and the y components separately: $R = \sqrt{(\Sigma X)^2 + (\Sigma Y)^2}$, $\tan\varphi = \Sigma Y/\Sigma X$.

cards.front_md: Define the scalar product and give an example from physics.
cards.back_md: $\vec{A}\cdot\vec{B} = AB\cos\theta$, a scalar; work $W = \vec{F}\cdot\vec{s}$.

cards.front_md: Write the dot product in components and the condition for perpendicular vectors.
cards.back_md: $A_xB_x + A_yB_y + A_zB_z$; perpendicular when it is zero.

cards.front_md: Define the vector product and give an example.
cards.back_md: $\vec{A}\times\vec{B} = AB\sin\theta\,\hat{n}$, a vector by the right-hand screw rule; torque $\vec{\tau} = \vec{r}\times\vec{F}$.

cards.front_md: Give the cross products of the unit vectors.
cards.back_md: $\hat{\imath}\times\hat{\jmath} = \hat{k}$, $\hat{\jmath}\times\hat{k} = \hat{\imath}$, $\hat{k}\times\hat{\imath} = \hat{\jmath}$; reversed order gives the negative; $\hat{\imath}\times\hat{\imath} = 0$.

cards.front_md: Is the cross product commutative?
cards.back_md: No: $\vec{B}\times\vec{A} = -(\vec{A}\times\vec{B})$.

cards.front_md: What are $\vec{A}\cdot\vec{B}$ and $|\vec{A}\times\vec{B}|$ at 0°, 90° and 180°?

questions.stem_md: Which statement about the null vector is correct?

options.text_md: It has zero magnitude and no definite direction, and adding it to any vector leaves that vector unchanged
It has zero magnitude and always points along the x-axis
It is the number zero, so it is a scalar
It has unit magnitude and no definite direction

questions.solution_md: The null vector has magnitude zero and no definite direction; A + 0 = A. It is a vector, not the number zero, and a unit magnitude would make it a unit vector.

provenance.author: claude-sonnet-5-5 (subject-producer chapter writer; reviewed by claude-opus-5-5)

questions.stem_md: A hockey stick strikes a ball. Which pair below contains only vector quantities?

options.text_md: Kinetic energy of the ball and work done by the stick
Momentum of the ball and force exerted by the stick
Speed of the ball and time of contact
Mass of the ball and power delivered by the player

questions.solution_md: Momentum and force have magnitude and direction. Kinetic energy, work, speed, time, mass and power are scalars.

provenance.author: claude-sonnet-5-5 (subject-producer chapter writer; reviewed by claude-opus-5-5)

questions.stem_md: Electric current flows in a definite direction along a wire, yet it is classified as a scalar. The reason is that

options.text_md: the direction of a current changes when the axes are rotated
its SI unit, the ampere, is a base unit
currents meeting at a junction add arithmetically and not by the parallelogram law
a current has a magnitude but is measured without any sign

questions.solution_md: A quantity is a vector only if it obeys the vector addition laws. Currents at a junction add as ordinary numbers, so current is a scalar although it has a sense along the wire.

provenance.author: claude-sonnet-5-5 (subject-producer chapter writer; reviewed by claude-opus-5-5)

questions.stem_md: A boat on a lake moves from the point (−2, 3) m to the point (4, −1) m, where the axes point east and north. Its displacement vector is
questions.solution_md: Displacement = final position − initial position = (4 + 2) î + (−1 − 3) ĵ = 6 î − 4 ĵ. Adding the two positions would give 2 î + 2 ĵ, and the displacement of the return trip would be −6 î + 4 ĵ.

provenance.author: claude-sonnet-5-5 (subject-producer chapter writer; reviewed by claude-opus-5-5)

questions.stem_md: Which of the following sets of vectors is always coplanar?

options.text_md: Three forces along the three edges of a cube that meet at one corner
The position vectors of any three points in space
A, B and A + B, for any two vectors A and B

questions.solution_md: The sum A + B lies in the plane of A and B. Three edges from one corner of a cube are mutually perpendicular, so they are not coplanar; three position vectors need not be; and A × B is perpendicular to the plane of A and B.

questions.solution_md: |A| = √(1² + 4² + 8²) = √81 = 9. Adding the components gives 13, and taking the root of 13 or stopping at 81 forgets one step.

questions.stem_md: The unit vector in the direction of −6î + 8ĵ is
questions.solution_md: |A| = √((−6)² + 8²) = 10. Dividing each component by 10 gives −0.6 î + 0.8 ĵ, whose magnitude is √(0.36 + 0.64) = 1. The vector −6î + 8ĵ itself has magnitude 10.

questions.solution_md: |A| = 3 and |λA| = |λ||A| = 3 × 3 = 9. The minus sign only reverses the direction; a magnitude is never negative.

provenance.author: claude-sonnet-5-5 (subject-producer chapter writer; reviewed by claude-opus-5-5)

questions.stem_md: Which statement about the unit vector î is correct?

options.text_md: It has the unit of the vector from which it is derived
It always has the same magnitude as the vector it describes
Its magnitude depends on the units of the axes
It has magnitude one, no dimensions and points along the positive x-axis

questions.solution_md: A unit vector is dimensionless and has magnitude exactly one. î is the unit vector along +x; ĵ and k̂ are along +y and +z.

questions.stem_md: The vectors 2î + 3ĵ and 6î + pĵ are parallel. The value of p is
questions.solution_md: Parallel vectors are multiples of each other: 6î + pĵ = λ(2î + 3ĵ) gives λ = 6/2 = 3 and p = 3 × 3 = 9.

questions.stem_md: Two forces of 9 N and 12 N act at a point at right angles to each other. The magnitude of their resultant is
questions.solution_md: For θ = 90°, R = √(A² + B²) = √(81 + 144) = 15 N. Adding magnitudes (21 N) is valid only for parallel forces.

provenance.author: claude-sonnet-5-5 (subject-producer chapter writer; reviewed by claude-opus-5-5)

questions.stem_md: Two vectors have magnitudes 12 and 5. The magnitude of their resultant can have any value from
questions.solution_md: R lies between |A − B| (opposite directions) and A + B (same direction): 7 to 17. It can be zero only if the two magnitudes are equal.

questions.stem_md: Two forces, each of magnitude F, act at a point with an angle of 120° between them. Their resultant has magnitude
questions.solution_md: R² = F² + F² + 2F·F cos 120° = 2F² − F² = F². For equal vectors R = 2F cos(θ/2) = 2F cos 60° = F.

marking_scheme.step: R² = F² + F² + 2F² cos 120° = F², so R = F (c)

questions.stem_md: Two forces of 5 N each act at a point, 60° apart. The resultant makes an angle with either force of
questions.solution_md: For equal vectors the resultant bisects the angle between them, so α = θ/2 = 30°. Direct calculation: tan α = (5 × 0.866)/(5 + 2.5) = 0.577.

provenance.author: claude-sonnet-5-5 (subject-producer chapter writer; reviewed by claude-opus-5-5)

questions.stem_md: Two vectors A and B have equal magnitudes of 10 units and the angle between them is 60°. The magnitude of A − B is
questions.solution_md: |A − B| = √(A² + B² − 2AB cos θ) = √(200 − 100) = 10. The value 17.32 would be |A + B|, and 20 would need θ = 180° for the difference.

provenance.author: claude-sonnet-5-5 (subject-producer chapter writer; reviewed by claude-opus-5-5)

questions.stem_md: Three forces act at a point. Which set of magnitudes can keep the point in equilibrium?
questions.solution_md: Three forces balance only if they can form a closed triangle, so each must be less than or equal to the sum of the other two. Only 4 N, 5 N and 8 N satisfies this (4 + 5 > 8); in each wrong set the largest force exceeds the sum of the other two.

provenance.author: claude-sonnet-5-5 (subject-producer chapter writer; reviewed by claude-opus-5-5)

questions.stem_md: Two forces acting at a point have a largest possible resultant of 18 N and a smallest possible resultant of 6 N. If the two forces are made to act at right angles to each other, their resultant is
questions.solution_md: The largest resultant is P + Q = 18 N and the smallest is P − Q = 6 N, so P = 12 N and Q = 6 N. At 90° R = √(P² + Q²) = √180 = 13.4 N.

marking_scheme.step: P + Q = 18 and P − Q = 6 give P = 12 N, Q = 6 N; R = √(12² + 6²) = 13.4 N (b)

questions.stem_md: A force of 10 N and a force of 6 N act at a point. The angle between them is adjusted until the resultant is perpendicular to the 6 N force. The angle between the two forces is then
questions.solution_md: The resultant R = A + B is perpendicular to B when R·B = 0, that is AB cos θ + B² = 0. Hence cos θ = −B/A = −0.6 and θ = 126.9°. The angle is obtuse because the larger force must pull back against the 6 N force; at 90° the resultant would lean towards the 10 N force.

marking_scheme.step: (A + B)·B = 0 gives AB cos θ + B² = 0, so cos θ = −6/10 and θ = 126.9° (d)

questions.solution_md: The angle is measured from the y-axis, so the component along y is A cos θ and the component along x is the side opposite the angle, A sin θ. Using A cos θ for x is the usual slip when the angle is from the other axis.

questions.stem_md: Two forces act on a point: 7 N along +x and 24 N along +y. Their resultant is
questions.solution_md: The forces are perpendicular, so R = √(49 + 576) = 25 N and tan φ = ΣY/ΣX = 24/7, giving φ = 73.7° from the x-axis.

questions.solution_md: Perpendicular vectors have a zero dot product: (2)(1) + (p)(−4) + (1)(2) = 4 − 4p = 0, so p = 1.

questions.stem_md: In a right-handed system of axes, k̂ × î equals
questions.solution_md: The cyclic order î → ĵ → k̂ → î gives î × ĵ = k̂, ĵ × k̂ = î and k̂ × î = ĵ. Reversing the order would give −ĵ.

questions.stem_md: The vector product of two non-zero vectors A and B is the null vector only when

options.text_md: A and B have equal magnitudes
A and B are parallel or antiparallel
A and B are drawn from the same point

questions.solution_md: |A × B| = AB sin θ is zero for non-zero vectors only if sin θ = 0, that is θ = 0° or 180°. For perpendicular vectors the cross product is largest.

options.text_md: A and B are parallel to each other
A and B have equal magnitudes
one of the vectors is a unit vector
A and B are perpendicular to each other

questions.solution_md: A·B = AB cos θ is zero with A and B non-zero only if cos θ = 0, that is θ = 90°.

questions.stem_md:
**Assertion (A):** A bus that returns to its starting stand after a round trip has a null displacement vector.

**Reason (R):** Displacement is the vector from the initial position to the final position, so it is zero when the two positions coincide.

Choose the correct option.

options.text_md: Both Assertion and Reason are true, and Reason is the correct explanation for Assertion.
Both Assertion and Reason are true, but Reason is not the correct explanation for Assertion.
Assertion is true and Reason is false.
Assertion is false and Reason is true.

questions.solution_md: A is true: the start and end positions are the same. R is true and gives exactly the reason, so R explains A.

provenance.author: claude-sonnet-5-5 (subject-producer chapter writer; reviewed by claude-opus-5-5)

questions.stem_md:
**Assertion (A):** Electric current is a scalar quantity although it is shown by an arrow in a circuit diagram.

**Reason (R):** The ampere, the SI unit of electric current, is one of the seven base units.

Choose the correct option.

options.text_md: Both Assertion and Reason are true, and Reason is the correct explanation for Assertion.
Both Assertion and Reason are true, but Reason is not the correct explanation for Assertion.
Assertion is true and Reason is false.
Assertion is false and Reason is true.

questions.solution_md: A is true: currents add arithmetically and do not obey the parallelogram law. R is also true, but being a base unit says nothing about whether a quantity is a scalar or a vector, so R does not explain A.

provenance.author: claude-sonnet-5-5 (subject-producer chapter writer; reviewed by claude-opus-5-5)

questions.stem_md:
**Assertion (A):** The magnitude of the sum of two vectors can be smaller than the magnitude of either vector.

**Reason (R):** Vectors are added by adding their magnitudes arithmetically.

Choose the correct option.

options.text_md: Both Assertion and Reason are true, and Reason is the correct explanation for Assertion.
Both Assertion and Reason are true, but Reason is not the correct explanation for Assertion.
Assertion is true and Reason is false.
Assertion is false and Reason is true.

questions.solution_md: A is true: for antiparallel vectors of magnitudes 5 and 6 the sum has magnitude 1, smaller than both. R is false: magnitudes add arithmetically only for vectors in the same direction. So A is true and R is false.

provenance.author: claude-sonnet-5-5 (subject-producer chapter writer; reviewed by claude-opus-5-5)

questions.stem_md:

questions.stem_md: A force F = 4î + 3ĵ newton moves a body through a displacement s = 6î + 2ĵ metre. Find the work done and the angle between the force and the displacement.

answer.model_answer_md: The work is the scalar product of force and displacement, found by multiplying the matching components and adding: $W = \vec{F}\cdot\vec{s} = (4)(6) + (3)(2) = 30$ J. The magnitudes are $F = \sqrt{16 + 9} = 5$ N and $s = \sqrt{36 + 4} = 6.325$ m, so $\cos\theta = 30/(5 \times 6.325) = 0.9487$ and the angle is $18.4^\circ$, which is acute because the work is positive.

questions.solution_md: Dot product of components, then arccos.

questions.stem_md: (a) Define a position vector and a displacement vector and state how they are related. [2] (b) A drone flies from the point P(3, −2, 5) m to the point Q(7, 1, 17) m. Find its displacement vector, the magnitude of the displacement and the unit vector along it. [3]

answer.model_answer_md:
(a) A position vector joins the origin to a point in space and tells where that point is. A displacement vector joins an initial position to a final position. It equals the final position vector minus the initial position vector, $\Delta\vec{r} = \vec{r}_2 - \vec{r}_1$, and depends only on the two end points, not on the path followed.

(b) Subtracting the coordinates of P from those of Q gives $\Delta\vec{r} = (7 - 3)\hat{\imath} + (1 + 2)\hat{\jmath} + (17 - 5)\hat{k} = 4\hat{\imath} + 3\hat{\jmath} + 12\hat{k}$ m. Its magnitude is the square root of the sum of the squares of the components, $\sqrt{16 + 9 + 144} = 13$ m. The unit vector along the displacement is found by dividing the displacement vector by this magnitude: $(4\hat{\imath} + 3\hat{\jmath} + 12\hat{k})/13$; it has magnitude one and no unit.

questions.solution_md: Final minus initial position; divide by the magnitude.

marking_scheme.step: Position vector: from the origin to the point
Displacement = r₂ − r₁, depends only on the end points

questions.stem_md: (a) State the parallelogram law of vector addition. [1] (b) Two vectors A and B act at a point with an angle θ between them. Derive an expression for the magnitude of the resultant R. [2] (c) Derive an expression for the angle α that R makes with A. [2]

answer.model_answer_md:
(a) If two vectors are drawn from a point as the adjacent sides of a parallelogram, their resultant is represented by the diagonal of the parallelogram through that point.

(b) Let $OP = A$, $PS = B$ and $OS = R$, and draw $SN$ perpendicular to $OP$ produced. In the triangle $PNS$, $PN = B\cos\theta$ and $SN = B\sin\theta$. In the right-angled triangle $ONS$, Pythagoras gives $R^2 = (A + B\cos\theta)^2 + (B\sin\theta)^2$, and since $\cos^2\theta + \sin^2\theta = 1$, $R = \sqrt{A^2 + B^2 + 2AB\cos\theta}$.

(c) In the same triangle the tangent of the angle $\alpha$ is the opposite side over the adjacent side: $\tan\alpha = \dfrac{SN}{ON} = \dfrac{B\sin\theta}{A + B\cos\theta}$, so $\alpha$ is measured from the vector $A$.

questions.solution_md: Perpendicular SN to OP produced; Pythagoras for R, tangent for α.

Figure with SN perpendicular to OP produced; PN = B cos θ, SN = B sin θ
tan α = SN/ON with ON = A + B cos θ
α = tan⁻¹[B sin θ/(A + B cos θ)]

questions.stem_md: (a) Write the magnitude of the resultant of two vectors A and B when the angle between them is (i) 0°, (ii) 90° and (iii) 180°, and say which gives the largest and the smallest value. [2] (b) Two forces of 8 N and 6 N act at a point with an angle of 60° between them. Find the magnitude of the resultant and its direction with respect to the 8 N force. [3]

answer.model_answer_md:
(a) Put each angle into $R = \sqrt{A^2 + B^2 + 2AB\cos\theta}$. (i) For parallel vectors the magnitudes simply add, $R = A + B$, the largest value. (ii) At right angles $R = \sqrt{A^2 + B^2}$. (iii) For opposite vectors the magnitudes subtract, $R = |A - B|$, the smallest value.

(b) Now apply the same law to the two forces given in the question, taking the 8 N force as the first vector. $R^2 = 8^2 + 6^2 + 2(8)(6)\cos 60^\circ = 64 + 36 + 48 = 148$, so $R = 12.17$ N. For the direction, $\tan\alpha = \dfrac{6\sin 60^\circ}{8 + 6\cos 60^\circ} = \dfrac{5.196}{11} = 0.4724$, so the resultant makes $25.3^\circ$ with the 8 N force. As expected, it lies between the two forces and nearer the larger one, and its magnitude is less than their arithmetic sum of 14 N.

questions.solution_md: Special angles in the general law; then R² and tan α for 8 N and 6 N.

questions.stem_md: (a) A force F acts at an angle θ to the x-axis. Write its rectangular components and show that they reproduce the magnitude of F. [2] (b) Three forces of 12 N, 16 N and 10 N act at a point in the directions 30°, 150° and 270° from the +x axis. Find the magnitude and direction of the resultant by resolving along the axes. [3]

answer.model_answer_md:
(a) Resolving along the axes gives $F_x = F\cos\theta$ and $F_y = F\sin\theta$. Squaring and adding the components, $F_x^2 + F_y^2 = F^2(\cos^2\theta + \sin^2\theta) = F^2$, so the components reproduce the magnitude of the force.

(b) Draw the three forces from the point, measure each angle from the +x axis, resolve every force along the two axes and add the components with their signs, taking care over which are negative. $\Sigma X = 12\cos 30^\circ + 16\cos 150^\circ + 10\cos 270^\circ = 10.39 - 13.86 + 0 = −3.464$ N and $\Sigma Y = 6 + 8 - 10 = 4.00$ N. The magnitude is $R = \sqrt{12.00 + 16.00} = 5.292$ N. Since $\Sigma X$ is negative and $\Sigma Y$ is positive, the resultant lies in the second quadrant, at $130.9^\circ$ from the $+x$ axis.

questions.solution_md: Resolve each force; the signs of the sums give the quadrant.

questions.stem_md: Two vectors are A = 3î − 2ĵ + 6k̂ and B = î + 2ĵ − 2k̂. (a) Find A + B and 2A − 3B. [2] (b) Find the magnitude of A + B. [1] (c) Find the magnitude of A and the angle that A makes with the z-axis. [2]

answer.model_answer_md:
(a) Add or subtract the vectors component by component. $\vec{A} + \vec{B} = (3 + 1)\hat{\imath} + (-2 + 2)\hat{\jmath} + (6 - 2)\hat{k} = 4\hat{\imath} + 4\hat{k}$, because the $\hat{\jmath}$ component cancels. For the second combination, multiply first and then subtract: $2\vec{A} - 3\vec{B} = (6 - 3)\hat{\imath} + (-4 - 6)\hat{\jmath} + (12 + 6)\hat{k} = 3\hat{\imath} - 10\hat{\jmath} + 18\hat{k}$.

(b) The magnitude is the square root of the sum of the squares of the components: $|\vec{A} + \vec{B}| = \sqrt{16 + 0 + 16} = \sqrt{32} = 5.657$.

(c) $|\vec{A}| = \sqrt{9 + 4 + 36} = 7$. The cosine of the angle with the z-axis is the z component divided by the magnitude, $\cos\gamma = 6/7$, so the angle with the z-axis is $31.0^\circ$.

questions.stem_md: (a) Define the scalar product of two vectors and state two of its properties. [2] (b) A force F = 5î + 2ĵ − 3k̂ newton displaces a body from the point (1, 2, 3) m to the point (4, 6, 5) m. Find the work done by the force. [2] (c) Find the angle between the force and the displacement. [1]

answer.model_answer_md:
(a) The scalar product is $\vec{A}\cdot\vec{B} = AB\cos\theta$, and the result is a scalar. Two properties: it is commutative, $\vec{A}\cdot\vec{B} = \vec{B}\cdot\vec{A}$, and distributive over addition; it is also zero for two perpendicular vectors.

(b) The displacement is the final position minus the initial position: $\vec{s} = (4 - 1)\hat{\imath} + (6 - 2)\hat{\jmath} + (5 - 3)\hat{k} = 3\hat{\imath} + 4\hat{\jmath} + 2\hat{k}$ m. The work done is the dot product of force and displacement, $W = (5)(3) + (2)(4) + (-3)(2) = 17$ J.

(c) The magnitudes are $F = \sqrt{38}$ N and $s = \sqrt{29}$ m, so $\cos\theta = 17/\sqrt{38 \times 29} = 0.5121$, which gives an angle of $59.2^\circ$ between the force and the displacement.

questions.solution_md: Displacement from the end points; dot product of components; arccos.

marking_scheme.step: A·B = AB cos θ, a scalar
Two properties (commutative, distributive, zero for perpendicular vectors)

questions.stem_md: (a) Define the vector product A × B and state how the direction of A × B is found. [2] (b) For A = 2î − ĵ + 3k̂ and B = î + 2ĵ − k̂ find A × B and verify that it is perpendicular to A. [2] (c) A force of 25 N is applied at right angles to a door at a point 0.4 m from the hinge. Find the magnitude of the torque. [1]

answer.model_answer_md:
(a) The vector product is $\vec{A}\times\vec{B} = AB\sin\theta\,\hat{n}$, a vector whose magnitude equals the area of the parallelogram on $\vec{A}$ and $\vec{B}$. Its direction $\hat{n}$ is perpendicular to both vectors, found by the right-hand screw rule: a right-handed screw turned from $\vec{A}$ towards $\vec{B}$ advances along $\hat{n}$.

(b) Using the determinant form, $\vec{A}\times\vec{B} = ((-1)(-1) - (3)(2))\hat{\imath} + ((3)(1) - (2)(-1))\hat{\jmath} + ((2)(2) - (-1)(1))\hat{k} = -5\hat{\imath} + 5\hat{\jmath} + 5\hat{k}$. To verify, $\vec{A}\cdot(\vec{A}\times\vec{B}) = (2)(-5) + (-1)(5) + (3)(5) = 0$, so the product is perpendicular to $\vec{A}$.

(c) The force is perpendicular to the lever arm, so $\tau = rF\sin 90^\circ = (0.4)(25) = 10$ N m.

questions.solution_md: Component formula, dot product zero check, τ = r F.

Direction by the right-hand screw rule, perpendicular to both
